analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from buying back their own stock and requires worker-elected seats on corporate boards.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have banned companies from buying back their own stock and required employee-elected board seats, was introduced in June 2018 and died in the House Financial Services Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Reward Work Act would do two things: make it illegal for publicly traded companies to buy back their own shares on the open market, and require any company listing its stock on a US exchange to reserve one-third of its board seats for directors elected by its employees, one employee one vote. The idea is that corporate cash now spent propping up stock prices — which benefits executives paid in stock and large shareholders — would instead be available for wages, investment, or dividends, and that workers would get a direct voice in the companies they work for.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at publicly traded companies, who would gain one-third of the seats on their employer's board, elected by employees alone. Ordinary savers and employees also hold shares through pensions and 401(k)s, and advocates argue the buyback ban would redirect corporate cash from stock-price support toward wages, investment, and dividends.

how_it_helps.text: It bars any public company from buying its own shares on a national securities exchange and voids the SEC rule (10b-18) that had given companies a safe harbor for such purchases.

It bars companies from registering securities on a national exchange unless at least one-third of their board of directors is elected by employees in a one-employee-one-vote election, with the SEC and NLRB writing rules to make those elections fair and to phase in employee representation within two years.

analysis.who_pays: Public-company executives and large shareholders, who benefit from buybacks that lift stock prices and executive stock-based pay, and who would lose the flexibility of repurchases. Boards would also share power with employee-elected directors.

drawbacks.text: An outright ban on open-market repurchases is blunt: companies would lose a standard, legal way to return cash to shareholders, which some economists argue benefits retirement savers and does not necessarily come at workers' expense.

Mandating employee-elected directors for every listed company is a major structural change to corporate governance whose effects on firm performance and capital raising were not tested through hearings, since the bill never received any.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits would be broad and the costs concentrated: employees would gain a durable voice in corporate governance and public companies would lose the ability to recycle cash into their own stock, with the money instead available for wages, investment, or dividends. The strongest good-faith objection is that the buyback ban is blunt — repurchases can be a legitimate way to return excess cash to shareholders, and the ban does not distinguish between manipulation and genuine capital allocation. The board-representation mandate is also a structural change whose effects on firm performance were untested in US markets. But since the bill never received a hearing or a vote, none of these tradeoffs were ever weighed in the record.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the term ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 13, 2018, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The committee held no markup, hearing on the bill, or floor vote; the Congress ended on January 3, 2019, killing the bill.
It attracted just one cosponsor, Rep. Ro Khanna.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporate executives and large shareholders are better off: buybacks remain legal and employee board representation was never enacted, so management keeps full control of corporate cash and boards.

for.name: Rep. Keith Ellison
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured a committee referral.

against.name: Corporate and financial industry interests
against.role: Business groups, major public companies, and the securities industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed buyback restrictions and mandatory worker board representation as a rule; buybacks remained legal and no similar measure advanced.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats, and the bill attracted a single cosponsor; no Republican supported it, and the Republican-controlled House Financial Services Committee never took it up.

industries.industry: Publicly traded corporations and their executives
industries.note: They would lose the ability to prop up share prices and support stock-based pay through open-market buybacks, and would have to give one-third of board seats to employee-elected directors. Both changes directly reduce management's discretion and shift power toward workers.

Buybacks are a major source of shareholder returns; banning them would shift corporate cash toward other uses, potentially including wages and investment, and remove the price support that buybacks provide to stock holdings.
Employees would gain a guaranteed one-third share of board seats, giving them a formal voice in decisions like pay, layoffs, and buybacks at the companies they work for.
